title: How do supermarkets make money, and what matters in a retail case?
description: Grocery retail economics for case interviews: thin margins, basket size, footfall, sales per square foot, private label and online delivery costs.
hook: Supermarkets run on very thin margins and huge volumes, so small changes matter enormously. A one-point change in margin can halve or double profit. Here is what drives a grocery business and how retail cases tend to work.
body:
The basic equation

Revenue = number of shopping trips × average basket. Profit depends on gross margin (price minus product cost) minus store, staff, logistics and online costs.

Thin margins

Many large grocers make operating margins of only a few percent. On £10B of sales, a 3% margin is £300M; a fall to 2% removes a third of profit, even if sales grow.

The levers

  • Footfall and basket size: how often people come and how much they buy.
  • Mix: fresh food, ready meals and own-label usually earn more than branded staples.
  • Private label: the retailer's own brand often earns a higher margin per item than big brands.
  • Shrinkage and waste: theft and food thrown away.
  • Space: sales per square foot shows which stores and aisles work hardest.

Online delivery

Picking and delivering an order costs a significant amount per order. If the average order is £80 and margin is 25%, gross profit is £20; if picking and delivery cost £15, little is left. That is why delivery fees and minimum baskets exist.

Typical retail case questions

  • Why has our margin fallen while sales grew?
  • Should we launch a premium own-label range?
  • Should we open dark stores for fast delivery?
  • How should we respond to a discounter entering our market?

Follow one basket all the way to profit

Suppose a supermarket sells a typical £50 basket and pays suppliers £37 for the products. Its gross profit is £13, or 26% of sales. From that £13 it still needs to cover employees, rent, energy, distribution, shrinkage and central overhead. If those costs amount to £11.50 per basket, operating profit is just £1.50, or a 3% operating margin. This is an illustrative store-level model, not an industry benchmark.

Now a competitor cuts its prices and the supermarket considers a 2% price reduction. That is £1 per basket. If supplier costs and other expenses are unchanged, profit falls from £1.50 to £0.50 per basket. The business would need three times as many baskets to preserve total operating profit at this contribution level. That is why small changes in price, product mix and waste can matter enormously in grocery retail.

When diagnosing store performance, separate footfall × purchase conversion × average basket, then look at gross margin and the operating cost per store. A shift towards low-margin promotions can increase revenue while reducing profit. A change in waste or theft can reduce profit without appearing in sales figures. Online delivery introduces a separate question: does the delivery fee cover picking, packing and the final mile, or does each order dilute store profitability?

Try this: a store has flat sales but operating profit halves. Ask for gross margin, waste and labour hours per £1,000 of sales before suggesting a marketing campaign.
